sub: English idioms borrow from sports and school all the time — 'hit the books,' 'drop the ball.' Read the clues, compare them across languages, and crack the locks.
kw: idioms sports school study ball hit the books drop the ball ballpark figure the ball is in your court english spanish pelota figurative language multilingual esl grade 6 7 8

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Name the source and the meaning
brief.p: You are reading idioms as figurative language — noticing HOW the phrase works, not whether the words are literally true. Find the meaning, use context, and compare across languages.

win.p: You separated the literal picture from the real meaning and compared languages. Noticing how figurative language works is a powerful reading skill.

clues.title: 'Hit the books'
clues.body: 'Hit the books' means to study hard — you don't actually hit anything. Spanish says 'ponerse a estudiar' or 'hincar los codos' (dig in the elbows) — a different picture, same idea.

clues.title: 'A ballpark figure'
clues.body: A 'ballpark figure' is a rough estimate, not an exact number. It comes from baseball. Spanish says 'una cifra aproximada' — no sports picture at all.

clues.title: 'Drop the ball'
clues.body: To 'drop the ball' means to make a mistake or fail a responsibility. Spanish says 'meter la pata' (put in the paw/foot) — a different picture, same idea: to mess up.

clues.title: 'The ball is in your court'
clues.body: 'The ball is in your court' means it is your turn to decide or act. Spanish says 'la pelota está en tu tejado' (the ball is on your roof) — the SAME ball, a different place.

clues.title: Idioms have sources
clues.body: Idioms often come from everyday life — sports, school, work. The same idea can keep the picture (ball → pelota) or change it entirely. Tracing the source is a reading skill.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: The largest stadium in the world holds about 114,000 people. That is a true sports fact — but it has nothing to do with what these idioms mean.

locks.title: What does it really mean?
locks.q: What does 'drop the ball' really mean?
options: To make a mistake or fail a responsibility
locks.reason: Clue 3 says it means to make a mistake. The literal picture — dropping a ball — is the trap. Idioms rarely mean what the words say.

locks.title: What is true about idioms?
locks.q: Check every statement that is TRUE (use the clues). Leave out the false one.

items.t: An idiom's meaning is not the sum of its words
English 'the ball is in your court' and Spanish 'la pelota está en tu tejado' both use a BALL
A 'ballpark figure' is a rough estimate, not an exact number
Every sports idiom is really about playing a sport

locks.reason: The false statement is the trap: the sport is a picture, not the meaning. The three true statements come straight from the clues.

locks.title: Put the talk in order
locks.q: Tap the three lines in the ORDER that makes 'the ball is in your court' make sense.

pads.e: 🤔 'So the ball is in my court now?'

locks.reason: The order shows the meaning: an offer is sent, the other person asks if it's their turn ('ball in my court'), and it's confirmed. Idioms depend on context.

locks.title: Compare the two languages
locks.q: Both idioms use the same sport object to mean 'it's your turn': English 'the ball is in your court,' Spanish 'la pelota está en tu tejado.' Type that object in English OR Spanish.
locks.reason: English 'ball,' Spanish 'pelota' — the same object, the same meaning: it's your turn to act. Comparing across languages sharpens the reading.

h1: Time & Money: Idioms That Cost You
sub: English treats time and money like objects — 'time flies,' 'break the bank.' Read the clues, compare them across languages, and crack the locks.
kw: idioms time money break the bank time flies once in a blue moon el tiempo vuela save time waste time english spanish metaphor figurative language multilingual esl grade 7 8

brief.label: Your mission
brief.h: Read time and money as metaphors
brief.p: English often treats time and money as if they were objects you can save, spend, or lose. Notice the metaphor, find the meaning, and compare across languages.

win.p: You read time and money as metaphors, found the meanings, and compared languages — strong figurative-language thinking.

clues.title: 'Time flies'
clues.body: 'Time flies' means time passes very quickly. Spanish says 'el tiempo vuela' (time flies) — the SAME picture: flying time!

clues.title: 'Break the bank'
clues.body: To 'break the bank' means to cost too much or use up all your money. Spanish says 'costar un dineral' (to cost a fortune) — a different picture, same idea: very expensive.

clues.title: 'Once in a blue moon'
clues.body: 'Once in a blue moon' means very rarely. Spanish says 'de vez en cuando' (from time to time) or 'de Pascuas a Ramos' — a different picture, same idea: rarely.

clues.title: Time acts like money
clues.body: In English you can 'save time,' 'spend time,' or 'waste time' — as if time were money. Spanish does this too: 'ahorrar tiempo' (save time), 'perder el tiempo' (waste time).

clues.title: The shared metaphor
clues.body: Many languages treat time like a resource you can save or spend. Some idioms keep the same picture (time flies = el tiempo vuela); some change it. Noticing the metaphor is a reading skill.

clues.title: True, but off-topic
clues.body: Diamonds are the hardest natural material on Earth. That is a true science fact — but it has nothing to do with what these idioms mean.

locks.title: What does it really mean?
locks.q: What does 'break the bank' really mean?
options: To cost too much or use up all your money
locks.reason: Clue 2 says it means to cost too much. The literal picture — robbing or breaking a bank — is the trap. Idioms rarely mean what the words say.

locks.title: What is true about idioms?
locks.q: Check every statement that is TRUE (use the clues). Leave out the false one.

items.t: An idiom's meaning is not the sum of its words
English 'time flies' and Spanish 'el tiempo vuela' use the SAME picture
'Once in a blue moon' means something happens very rarely
'Break the bank' means to actually rob a bank

locks.reason: The false statement is the trap: 'break the bank' is a metaphor for cost, not a real robbery. The three true statements come straight from the clues.

locks.title: Put the talk in order
locks.q: Tap the three lines in the ORDER that makes 'once in a blue moon' make sense.

pads.e: 🙂 'No — only once in a blue moon.'
🍦 'Do you eat ice cream every day?'

locks.reason: The order shows the meaning: a question, the reply 'once in a blue moon,' and the paraphrase 'almost never.' Context is what unlocks an idiom.

locks.title: Compare the two languages
locks.q: In English, time passes fast when 'time ___.' In Spanish, 'el tiempo ___' (vuela). Both use the SAME picture. Type the action in English OR Spanish.
locks.reason: English 'flies,' Spanish 'vuela' — the same picture (flying) for time passing fast. When the metaphor matches across languages, it is easy to remember.
